In this study, we investigate and address a prevalent issue in solar physics - the introduction of artificial magnetic field patterns resulting from inaccurate magnetograph measurements. These artifacts, such as wave-like structures and alternating polarity signs, are typically associated with incorrect data and can be identified through specific criteria. We have developed a machine learning-based algorithm to automatically detect these artifacts in the magnetic field data. The proposed method, which is relatively simple and computationally efficient, has been applied to the Solar Dynamics Observatory's HMI and the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope's spectropolarimetric observations. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in identifying and mitigating artifacts, thereby enhancing the accuracy of magnetic field estimates.

A primary factor contributing to the instability of smart grids is the uncontrolled demand side, which can be effectively stabilized through demand side control (DSC). By incorporating DSC, a method is proposed to address the power system's uncertainty. Focusing on user comfort, this study presents an independent DSC approach that utilizes energy usage planning (EUP) and real-time load charging (RLC). By applying collective games, a unified solution is achieved for coordinating energy usage planning among real-time load charging users. Furthermore, an artificial neural network is employed to facilitate real-time load charging. Simulation results demonstrate the proposed approach's ability to mitigate the power system's uncertainty and optimize energy distribution in real-time.

The astrophysical properties of compact celestial bodies are determined by their gravitational effects on emitted radiation, particularly the interplay between the radiation's energy and the gravitational field. A study examining the Rastall theory of gravity, specifically black hole solutions with electric charges, aims to understand how the gravitational influence affects Hawking emission, thereby shedding light on the thermodynamic behavior of these compact celestial bodies. The analysis involves investigating the temperature, evaporation rate, and remaining lifespan of the black holes, which in turn provides insight into their lifecycle and eventual death.

We apply functional law of the iterated logarithm and strong invariance principle to the spectral distribution in von Neumann's Ergodic theorem, thereby deriving a precise evaluation of its convergence speed. Furthermore, we establish functional law of the iterated logarithm for the empirical spectral distribution (ESD) arising from Arakova and Liang's quadratic form chunked Gaussian random matrices, which have non-i.i.d. entries. It is noteworthy that the presence of non-i.i.d. entries and the utilization of a quadratic form necessitate the adoption of a more sophisticated approach, specifically the approach developed by Arakova and Liang, in contrast to the standard methodologies employed for classical random matrices with i.i.d. entries.

The recently acquired spectra from the Gaia BP/RP photometric system can be utilized to analyze the properties of metal-poor stars. By employing a specific subset of 10 BP/RP spectral features, we were able to directly estimate the metallicity of these stars. It has been observed that the developed technique is effective for stars with a specific range of temperatures and metallicities, and it has been tested for a sample of 100000 stars. It was found that the method is suitable for A/F type stars with low metallicity and it has been observed that the metallicity estimates of the developed technique are consistent with the ones obtained using the Gaia-EHR spectroscopic survey for a subset of 100000000 stars. Furthermore, it was found that the developed technique is capable of distinguishing between certain types of stars and it has been observed that the developed technique is sensitive to the radial velocity of the stars. Lastly, it was found that the developed technique has been applied to the Gaia-ESO survey and it has been observed that the developed technique is capable of recovering the metallicity of the stars in the Gaia-ESO survey.

Every year, wildfires ravage numerous regions across the globe, causing extensive damage to life and property. Although studies have linked annual fire outbreaks to climate change, no precise measurement of fire season intensity has been developed. To address this gap, a novel approach utilizing data from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) has been proposed to assess fire season intensity globally, thereby enabling researchers to evaluate the impact of climate change on wildfire outbreaks. By analyzing MODIS data from 2001 to 2019, a Worldwide Fire Season Intensity Assessment and Prediction (WFSIAP) model was developed, which accurately predicts fire season intensity in any given location. The results show that temperature and humidity significantly influence fire season intensity, and this impact is amplified in areas with longer fire seasons. Furthermore, projections based on the CMIP6 climate models indicate an increase in global fire season intensity by the end of the 21st century, with a more pronounced effect in areas experiencing longer fire seasons.

Language complexity is a crucial aspect that must be understood in various contexts, such as theoretical research and practical applications. Theoretical studies often analyze complexity in languages, while practical applications require the development of methods to measure and control complexity. To address this need, a recent study utilized data from 120 languages to create and validate metrics for assessing morphological complexity. The research involved developing a mathematical model to predict the complexity of morphological patterns within each language, and then tested the model's effectiveness by splitting the data into training and testing sets. The results showed that certain complexity metrics, like those based on morpheme frequency and lexical richness, performed better than others in predicting actual complexity. The study also found that a measure of cognitive effort, known as the $C^2$ metric, had significant practical applications. The research demonstrated the effectiveness of using cross-validation techniques to evaluate and compare complexity metrics, and highlighted the potential for such metrics to be used in linguistic studies and practical applications.

Researchers examining gravitational lensing effects in multiple galaxy clusters have discovered smaller caustics in their results. This discovery is inconsistent with the $\Lambda$CDM model, but could be explained by self-interacting dark matter. The size of these caustics can be used to estimate self-interacting dark matter's cross-section, with values ranging from 0.25 to 1.8 kiloparsecs. This range of values is consistent with observations of the dwarf galaxy Leo I and could resolve small-scale anomalies.

Model compression techniques have been utilized to reduce the computational requirements of complex neural networks, enabling their deployment on devices with limited resources. However, these methods typically assume full model visibility. In contrast, this paper investigates model compression with restricted access to a neural network, simulating scenarios in which only a portion of the model can be accessed. Our approach involves a two-stage process: first, we identify the most valuable sub-network components and retain them, while discarding the rest. Next, we train the retained sub-network from a shortened training sequence. Model averaging is employed to mitigate training inconsistencies. Experimental results on a variety of computer vision tasks demonstrate that this sub-network selection method outperforms comparable state-of-the-art compression methods.

M-estimation, a versatile method widely used in robust M-estimation independent component analysis, has been extensively studied in statistics.  However, the development of rapid independent component analysis algorithms for M-estimation has been a long-standing challenge, with the existing literature offering no solution.  In contrast, the speed of conventional ICA algorithms has been well-established.  This paper introduces M-ar-Rapid ICA, a new M-estimation ICA algorithm designed to address this issue.  By integrating elements from the m-RAPID algorithm and the BPDN algorithm, the M-ar-RAPID algorithm achieves a significant improvement in computational efficiency.  This advancement is further enhanced by the development of a rapid analytic backpropagation algorithm for M-estimation, which builds on the arithmetic rapid backpropagation method.  Through simulation studies, the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm is validated, with results demonstrating its superior performance in terms of model estimation accuracy and computational efficiency.

Traffic incidents on urban roads can cause substantial delays and increased emissions,
which is why they need to be identified and managed promptly to minimize congestion.
Socially tagged traffic updates can provide valuable real-time information,
aiding in the detection of incidents and reducing overall impact. To leverage this
informal yet timely data, we have developed a data-driven approach using
地理位置标记的交通数据 to identify socially tagged traffic incidents.
By analyzing users' shared images and text on platforms like Flickr and Twitter,
we can pinpoint and categorize incidents on specific road segments and types.
Our method achieves this by using machine learning to process the tagged data,
which enables the detection of incidents and reduction of false positives.
Experimental validation on a large dataset of 2018 social tag updates from San Francisco
reveals that our approach can accurately identify 98.5% of incident-related posts,
outperforming previous methods by 10% and 15% respectively.

The paper addresses an elliptic partial differential equation that incorporates a Radon measure on the boundary of the domain as the right-hand side. This equation involves functions with specific regularity on the boundary that can be either affine functions or more general functions defined in the domain extended with zero on the boundary. By utilizing the duality method, it is demonstrated that solutions to this equation exist and are unique. Furthermore, it is shown that even when the equation's coefficient matrix is not uniformly elliptic, solutions can still be obtained under certain conditions. To achieve this, a new inequality on the boundary is established, which is essential in proving the main results. Additionally, by employing a smooth approximation of the boundary functions, it is demonstrated that the obtained solutions are stable with respect to the equation's parameters.

Firstly, we utilized genetic algorithms to explore the yttrium-cobalt-boron system for unique and potentially stable materials. This was done by randomly selecting compositions and structures, which were then screened for thermodynamic stability. As a result, 12 novel cobalt-rich compounds were identified, 10 of which had not been previously reported. Furthermore, experimental validation confirmed the existence of 8 out of these 10 cobalt-rich Y-Co-B compounds. Lastly, our calculations suggest that the remaining two validated cobalt-rich compounds could be synthesized by reacting Y, Co, and B powders under specific conditions.

Real-time bidding has become the primary method for acquiring online ad impressions, where advertisers submit immediate bids for each impression within strict time constraints. Although predictive models can help determine the optimal price, they often overlook an advertiser's budget limitation, leading to ineffective spending strategies. In this research, we develop an algorithm that enables budget-conscious bidding, aiming to maximize the total value within budget constraints in real-time. The algorithm's theoretical and empirical results show that it can achieve a 5-10% improvement in expenditure efficiency over current solutions.

Regions with negative Wigner functions are often thought to inherently lack a interpretation in terms of phase space concepts and quantum processes. Our study demonstrates that these areas of negativity can be utilized to create phase-spaces that exhibit unique properties not found in classical concepts, such as causal time evolution. The project involves extracting information from quantum systems and applying it to 'guide' a classical system through the complex environment. The classical system is given instructions via messages, which enable it to navigate around the problematic areas of the phase-space, avoiding its negative aspects. The successful navigation of this process is accompanied by the restoration of Wigner positivity and the increase of mutual information between the quantum and classical systems, which can be measured by classical observables. The concept of quantum guidance has a dual meaning: it refers to the classical agent being guided by the quantum system, but also to the classical agent guiding the quantum system, measured by an observable, towards a desired state, such as the ground state. Our research showcases the potential of quantum-classical hybrid strategies in achieving tasks that a classical concept alone would find impossible, such as achieving quantum state ground preparation.

Quantum key distribution (QKD) systems are susceptible to attacks on the final stages, where pre-extracted randomness is used for verification and parameter estimation. A common approach to mitigate these vulnerabilities is to implement privacy amplification, which removes potential eavesdropped information. However, current security models often assume an ideal, uniformly distributed source of privacy amplification, which may not always be the case in practical settings. In this study, we derive a new security bound for BB84 QKD systems that accounts for non-uniform source distributions and attacks on the post-processing step. Our results reveal that taking the non-uniform source into account can lead to a more stringent security analysis, which may either tighten or loosen the security bound depending on the specific parameters used. This research contributes to a better understanding of practical QKD systems and their security guarantees in real-world applications.
This study investigates the timelike Bertrand conditions within a 3-dimensional semi-Riemannian manifold equipped with a local co-frame, and identifies their non-trivial solutions.

This paper investigates novel stochastic processes derived from the Feller diffusion, specifically examining Feller processes with comb and parabolic yield rates. The underlying processes are characterized as time-changed subordinated processes. A key finding is that Feller processes with the parabolic yield rate correspond to Feller diffusions time-subordinated by $1/4$-stable subordination. The Feller process with the parabolic yield rate is shown to be expressible as the sum of two independent, identically distributed Feller processes, each with parabolic yield rates. The paper also establishes that Feller processes with the parabolic yield rate cannot be expressed as the sum of two independent, non-identical Feller processes. The Feller process distribution is found to be Feller-distributed with modified parameters. The Feller process can be viewed as a time-subordinated Feller distribution, and under certain conditions, it is demonstrated that the Feller process with the parabolic yield rate has an unbounded number of summands in its representation as the sum of independent, non-identically distributed Feller processes. The paper also explores the properties of Feller processes under the operation of fractional powers. The study relies on the properties of Laplace transforms and the semigroups associated with the Feller diffusion, with the underlying Feller diffusion being the diffusion limit of the Wright-Fisher model.

We introduce an innovative approach to examining quantum scattering involving multiple photons and a single emitter confined within a photonic crystal waveguide. By leveraging a traditional many-body technique originally intended for bulk photonic systems, we can effectively model the unique behavior of an embedded emitter in nanophotonic devices where non-local interactions are significant. This method enables us to establish a systematic framework for analyzing the process, incorporating a single expansion parameter, and accurately account for all relevant effects. Furthermore, we apply this approach to investigate the properties of an emitter functioning as a single-photon beam splitter, exploring the breakdown of this ideal behavior in the presence of multiple incident photons. Our findings are then compared with numerical simulations and experimental data, highlighting the method's capability to provide an in-depth understanding of multi-photon scattering processes within these complex nanophotonic systems.

In the context of Dirac's dualistic model, where the vacuum's properties are influenced by the trace of the gamma matrices, the postulated boost-dependent Dirac action leads to the prediction of a time-varying gravitational potential. This theory aligns with General Relativity, while also introducing a spin-dependent gravitational redshift effect. Furthermore, the model suggests a coupling between the vacuum and fermions, which generates a force proportional to the fermion's mass. This force's influence is significant on sub-Hubble scales, but diminishes on larger scales, resulting in a modulated super-Hubble structure. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the vacuum-fermion interaction's impact on large-scale structure is substantial, thereby providing a means to test Dirac's model.
We discuss Faulhaber's discovery that odd power sums can be written as combinations of monomial sums, and how this formula generalizes to all prime powers using Fermat's Last Theorem.

This paper examines the performance of differential modulation through Continuous Phase Modulation (CPM) with non-coherent detection, focusing on its balance between distance, complexity, and bandwidth efficiency. A novel approach is introduced to enhance the distance properties of this type of modulation by leveraging the properties of Gray codes, resulting in improved differential CPM detection. Simulation results demonstrate that this novel approach yields a significant reduction in the error probability while maintaining similar spectral efficiency and transmission bandwidth, effectively reducing the distance properties by up to 3dB.

A key challenge in training reward models for reward-based reinforcement learning is the labor-intensive task of manually creating annotated datasets. To address this issue, we propose an approach that leverages human feedback on image quality to train a reward model. This quality is defined as visual attractiveness and technical correctness, two criteria that are orthogonal to each other. To address the scalability problem, we break down the feedback process into smaller tasks and incorporate visual aids to guide human evaluators. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we compare it to existing methods on three game environments and find that our reward model, trained using image-based evaluations, performs competitively with policy gradients trained using traditional reward models, while also outperforming them in scenarios with high sample efficiency.

This study explores the impact of noncommutative spacetime on the internal structure of nucleons, focusing on the deformation effects within the  $O(\theta)$  framework.  We examine how noncommutativity alters the nucleon's point form, ground state, and configuration functions, revealing that $\theta$-deformations modify spatial distributions and correlations of quarks in nucleons.  We also investigate the implications for the proton's structure function $G_E^{(3)}(x)$ and parton distribution functions.  To account for noncommutative spacetime, we utilize the Moyal product in spinor fields, ensuring that spinor algebra remains consistent.  We also establish spinor commutativity relations and derive the properties of derivatives in this context.  These findings are crucial for understanding the internal dynamics of nucleons in noncommutative spacetimes.

In a toroidal code model with frustation situated on a torus, our investigation focuses on the topological edge states that occur when atypical star or plaquette operators are applied on the boundary of the torus. By conducting an in-depth analysis of the stabilizer structure and measurement outcomes, we discovered that, in the absence of the $Z$-operation, the system reduces to two independent repetition codes. This results in a scenario where two qubits are utilized to describe the system's four logical states. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the system's four edge states are uniquely defined by four mutually orthogonal, local operator eigenstates. These findings are substantiated by numerical calculations.

We establish a set of basic eigenvalue bounds for the Hermitian part of typical random band matrices, modified by a self-energy perturbation of limited rank. Our results are consistent with an previously proposed light-cone effective medium theory, validated in a simplified form. Additionally, this work enhances the existing understanding of the spectral properties of random band matrices.

Recent advancements in the field of language models have led to remarkable breakthroughs in conversation understanding, yet these models are often hindered by their dependence on word embeddings that fail to capture linguistic semantics effectively. To address this issue, we introduce the concept of meaningful-based pre-training, which utilizes language models pre-trained with word and sentence embeddings to bridge the gap between these two representations. Our proposed MeaningoSentence pre-training task leverages the pre-trained model to generate meaningful representations of conversation sentences, which in turn enables superior performance in conversation comprehension. Our results demonstrate that this approach is particularly effective for conversations, where sentence context plays a pivotal role, and we further validate its capabilities by applying it to new domains and datasets.

As machine learning and artificial intelligence become increasingly integral to human lives, the need for transparency and clarity in the algorithms driving these systems has grown. This study presents a comprehensive framework for evaluating the understandability of algorithms from a human learning perspective. It also introduces a set of metrics to measure the complexity of learning and the difficulty of an algorithm, which can be applied to any learning task. Furthermore, we introduce a framework to identify and categorize the key factors that affect the learnability of any given problem, and we use this to introduce a metric to measure the difficulty of learning for any algorithm. This measure, known as the Cognitive Intricacy Score, is based on a set of criteria that assess the difficulty of learning for any algorithm. We then apply this metric to compare the complexity of learning for a range of algorithms, and we introduce a set of tools to measure the complexity of learning for any algorithm. Our work provides a framework for transparency and clarity in the machine learning and artificial intelligence communities, and we hope that this will contribute to the development of more interpretable and transparent algorithms.

An unsupervised algorithm called the Random Forest (RF) has been widely used in various applications. One of its key components, Isolation Tree (i-Tree), is an isolation forest (IForest) node that provides accurate anomaly detection performance. I-Tree offers faster training and inference times compared to RF node. However, I-Tree has not been extensively studied in the field of anomaly detection. This paper introduces a novel Isolation Tree with Weakly Guided Structure (TiWS-iTree) and its corresponding anomaly detection method, the Ti-forest. The proposed Ti-forest surpasses existing isolation forest and compressed isolation forest algorithms in terms of accuracy and efficiency. The experiments demonstrate that Ti-forest can achieve the same accuracy as compressed isolation forest with significantly reduced storage and computation requirements. The paper also provides implementation details and code for Ti-forest.

A novel, flexible Bayesian time-dependent extreme value model is introduced, which treats the time-varying log-gamma extreme value process as a Poisson process. This approach allows for a comprehensive Bayesian analysis of extreme value processes, where the arrival times of extreme events are parameterized in a meaningful way. This model is versatile and can be extended to model multiple types of processes occurring simultaneously. By deriving an explicit expression for the joint distribution of the processes, sampling from the joint posterior distribution is feasible through standard data augmentation techniques. This model is validated through a simulation study and further applied to model the complex process of COVID-19 cases in the UK.

The mathematical expression for total cross-section is fundamentally tied to an integral of the T-matrix over a 4-dimensional space, with the integration weights representing experimentally accessible scattering information. This chapter outlines a novel method to identify regions within the phase space where the total cross-section, or parts thereof, remains stationary under variations of the incident particle's energy or angular momentum. This approach enables a more profound understanding of the underlying scattering mechanisms.

This study presents COMET-ATOMIC, an enhanced and machine-learned model of the open common-sense knowledge graph ATOMIC. COMET-ATOMIC refines ATOMIC's knowledge through symbolic completion, eliminating contradictions, and contradications, as well as inferred relationships. Furthermore, the integration of deep neural networks enables the completion of ATOMIC's missing knowledge and the addition of weighted confidence scores to its assertions. COMET-ATOMIC surpasses the original graph in performance on tasks including question answering, fact checking, and knowledge completion.

An extensive photometric study, Hi-GAL, is being conducted to survey Galactic thermal emission at 652, 449, 255 and 190 micrometers. Utilizing the Herschel Space Observatory's PACS and SPIRE instruments, the survey covers the inner Galactic region, extending from latitude |b| > 2 degrees, across the full longitude. The Hi-GAL survey aims to identify thermal emission from star-forming regions in the galaxy, by classifying the emission into three categories: ULIRCs (Ultra Luminous Red Circles), ULBCHs (Ultra Luminous Bright Brightness Centers) and SiO maser sources. The survey's data processing is outlined in this document, detailing the reduction of raw images to final data products, including image reduction, source detection, and photometry extraction. The described reduction process is applicable to all Hi-GAL survey data, and the corresponding software is available for public use.

The globular cluster NGC 2808, which contains a variety of stars with different metal content levels, has intrigued astronomers because of its unusual composition. To better understand this unique star cluster, researchers used a sophisticated method to analyze the metal content of numerous stars, which had previously been unclear. Using high-resolution spectroscopy, they analyzed a total of 108 stars, which allowed them to establish a metal content range of 0.003 to 0.004. The results showed that there is a clear variation in metal content within the cluster, which is consistent with earlier research. The researchers also found that a new method for determining metal content, called iCaHK, yields similar results to another established method. The study concludes that there is a clear variation in metal content within NGC 2808, which is consistent with previous research.

In a single file diffusion process, the analysis of the distribution of exit times is crucial, and researchers have studied its variations based on different particle number scales. A detailed investigation of these variations has been conducted, and its implications on the single file diffusion process have been explored. By applying large deviation theory, it has been shown how these entropy-driven influences on exit times are connected to the dynamics within the file. Specifically, the entropy-driven component of the distribution is related to the distribution of the maximum displacement of the leading particle, and this has been confirmed through numerical simulations. A theoretical model has been proposed, and it suggests that the entropy-driven component of the distribution is directly connected to the distribution of the maximum displacement of the leading particle. These findings provide a deeper understanding of the single file diffusion process and its underlying entropy-driven mechanisms.

Quantum mechanics' non-commutative property renders the application of Bayes' theorem problematic due to the requirement of classical events for its validity. This study proposes a quantum extension of Bayes' theorem, which, for small probabilities, reduces to the original formulation. This quantum version resolves the inconsistency in quantum mechanics that arises from counterintuitive measurement results, such as those seen in the Hardy paradox and the GHZ paradox.

We introduce modified versions of an approximate Bayesian inference method to analyze the inverse participation ratio distributions from chiral random matrix theory ensembles through precise and efficient computational processes. The resulting data has been utilized to investigate the properties of quark number susceptibility in the random matrix models and in systems containing less than 3 linearly-sized color deconfinement units, which has not been thoroughly examined by previous analytical or numerical studies. We discover a significant discrepancy between the quark number susceptibility in tiny systems and its bulk limit. The introduction of a finite-size correction term to the equation of state for tiny systems is suggested, which is determined using ABC inference and matches the predictions from perturbation theory.

In modular cohomology groups of the Steenrod algebra, not every module is equivalent, and not every module can be expressed as a straightforward composition series. Although it has been established that the algebra is finite, not local, it remains an open question whether the composition factors in the cohomology groups form a finite collection. This paper presents an examination of the composition factors in $H^{s,w}(\mathop{\rm Ht}\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\mathop{\rm }\

Recent breakthroughs in filter technology have made it possible to develop a compact, lightweight Lyman-alpha filter that operates across a broad wavelength range. A model has been designed that mimics this filter's transmission and polarization characteristics. By expanding the filter's bandwidth, scientists can observe a wider area of space, including regions with lower star formation rates. A model has been developed that accurately predicts the performance of an LY1-like filter across various photometric bands. This could enable new space missions to collect more data on star-forming galaxies across a broader range of areas.

This research investigates the issue of regulated output tracking in distributed and interconnected network systems characterized by symmetry. We begin by examining the properties of permitted graph filters in representing symmetric networks and how these filters can be decomposed into a product of block-circulant filters and a permutation matrix. This choice is motivated by the potential for each node to implement these filters using a relatively compact number of non-local operations. This representation allows us to formulate tracking objectives as a multi-agent optimization problem, which can be efficiently resolved through an optimized version of the alternating direction method of multipliers. This proposed solution is then validated through numerical experiments.

Retrieving information from visual content has been extensively researched, but
most approaches focus on retrieving a single image.  In contrast, video retrieval
poses a unique challenge due to its dynamic nature, where extracting and
analyzing relevant information requires identifying and extracting information
from individual frames.  In addition to retrieving a single image, the problem
involves identifying the number of relevant frames and selecting the most
informative ones.  This paper presents a novel method for creating an adaptive
visual index, tailored to extract information from individual frames and
create a hierarchical representation.  This index is then used to design two
efficient retrieval systems - one for retrieving relevant frames and another
for retrieving a single video.  Our approach outperforms existing methods in
retrieval performance, particularly when the query contains multiple objects.

This paper introduces a reliable authentication system for the Gaussian noise waveform itself, which can serve as a verification tool in situations where sharing a secret key is not an option. The concept of using the Gaussian noise waveform as a shared secret is then explored through secure communication over a noisy channel without requiring a pre-shared key. The proposed protocols are demonstrated to be secure, and a specific achievable rate for communicating in this scenario is identified and shown to approach the channel capacity as the shared secret's entropy tends towards infinity.

We analyze and simulate 1D chains with hard-wall washboard potentials, observing uniform transport under various loading conditions. This is confirmed through numerical and analytical models that consider the dynamics of particle collisions, consistent with analytical models based on mean transport theory. The point of zero loading is also identified as critical in determining total and fluctuating transport.

This study introduces an adaptable approach to estimating impulse response functions, which are a crucial element in economic analysis, by a modification of Chudik et al. (2021)'s research. The adaptation is made to the original projection estimator, which is known to be a form of local linear regression, to handle instances where the local polynomial fit is inadequate, resulting in higher bias. The enhanced estimator is then proven to maintain the optimal root mean squared error rate, which was initially established by Chudik et al. (2021). The convergence rate of the new estimator is also determined, and simulations show that it performs comparably to the local projections method in cases where it is successful and outperforms it in scenarios where higher bias is expected due to local polynomial regression. The results are further supported by an application of the method in economic research from Bernanke et al. (1997) and from another analysis of the stock market reaction to monetary policy surprises, which can be found in Gilchrist and Zakrajsek (2009).

We have calculated the angular Casimir Poincaré stress tensor for an electric charge at rest in a constant magnetic field. This is the first such calculation for a particle subject to a non-uniform force. We have also determined the particle's mass shift due to this angular Casimir momentum.

The primary goal of Named Entity Recognition (NER) is to identify and classify entities, breaking them down into smaller, more detailed subcategories. A key challenge in NER lies in accurately detecting fine-grained entity types, given the inherent ambiguity of language. To overcome this problem, we introduce FGNET-RH, a novel framework for refining named entity classification within a hyperbolic space. Leveraging the inherent structure of hyperbolic space, FGNET-RH is capable of capturing hierarchical relationships among entity types, thus facilitating more accurate recognition. Furthermore, FGNET-RH employs a refinement mechanism to enhance its ability to distinguish between similar entity types. Our experimental results on NER datasets reveal that FGNET-RH outperforms existing baselines, especially in fine-grained entity classification.
The maximal value of the second Hankel determinant for general univalent functions and functions belonging to the class U has been determined.

To optimize resource allocation for virtual machine data center services, we introduce Prepartition, a novel load distribution approach. Lacking full knowledge of future requests, Prepartition initially estimates the required resources for VMs and allocates them in discrete units of minimum 'granules'. It then distributes the allocated granules evenly across servers, ensuring no server is overloaded. Subsequent steps involve scheduling actual VMs onto these servers, while handling any excess on a first-come, first-served basis. Our extensive simulations, incorporating real-world request patterns, demonstrate Prepartition's superiority over random and first-come, first-served scheduling methods in terms of maximizing the number of scheduled VMs and minimizing the average time each VM spends running on a server.

In many strategic games, unpredictable actions and unknown strategies make it challenging to find an exact equilibrium, especially in games with continuous variables. To address this, our approach involves predicting player behaviors and anticipating game outcomes, which enables efficient approximation of equilibrium solutions. Our proposed method, a Fixed Point Network (FPNet), is designed to learn and forecast equilibrium characteristics by iteratively refining estimates based on learned fixed points. Our results show that FPNet can successfully learn and generalize equilibrium behaviors across a wide range of adversarial and non-adversarial games, and our outcomes in simulated and real-world traffic control scenarios demonstrate its practical value.

A new, statistically sound restriction is established on a specific type of average impact measurement, which is particularly beneficial in fields such as medicine and marketing. Under certain conditions, this average impact can be precisely calculated from the available data. However, when the 'consistent effect' assumption is not met, any estimator of the average impact will introduce bias. A broader class of estimators is therefore proposed, which provides an upper limit on the absolute value of the bias. This class includes widely recognized methods, such as LASSO and Graphical LASSO. Through simulations, the accuracy of these estimators is demonstrated when estimating a particular effect measurement in artificial data sets.

This study introduces a method for conducting predictive analysis in industrial systems to detect ongoing cyber attacks. We consider a scenario where an adversary successfully conceals their actions from real-time monitoring by launching a linear, non time-varying cyber attack on a linear system. We demonstrate that when such an attack is hidden, there are limited opportunities for detecting it using real-time monitoring. However, by utilizing future system data and sensor readings, our proposed approach can accurately identify active cyber attacks within a short time frame. We have mathematically demonstrated the ability of our method to detect attacks and further showed that using predictive analysis significantly decreases false alarm rates while maintaining attack detection rates. Additionally, our research was validated through a simulation of a steam generator system.

This paper introduces GAE-ISumm, a state-of-the-art graph-based model for multi-document summarization specifically designed for Indian languages. Monitored Indian languages are largely dependent on English, resulting in limited data and resources available for summarization across the remaining 21 languages. To address this issue, we utilize transfer learning, fine-tuning our model on monitored Indian languages before adapting it to less monitored languages. This approach allows GAE-ISumm to achieve significant improvements over existing graph-based and transformer-based models, as evidenced by our results on four Indian language datasets. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of GAE-ISumm on low-resource datasets for Bengali and Bodo languages, which are among the least monitored Indian languages.

We have developed a definition of s-rings of Noether type and proved that the free s-continuous image of a Noether s-ring remains a Noether s-ring under the same definition. Consequently, it is also demonstrated that s-rings of this definition, derived from s-ring actions on sets, possess Noether property. Furthermore, it is also shown that the direct sum of two Noether s-rings of this definition retains the Noether property under this definition as well.

A recent investigation has uncovered a potential hidden mass influence in the orbits of five stars, which could be attributed to either dark matter or unobserved companions. By employing numerical simulations of dark matter subhaloes, we've determined that these observations cannot be accounted for by field subhaloes of a standard cosmological model, nor can they be explained by a single subhalo. Consequently, the observed deviations in the orbits of the five stars are consistent with the presence of one or more low-mass, undiscovered companion stars, which have hidden masses ranging from approximately 0.001 to 1000 solar masses, and distances of up to 1000 AU from the central stars. These constraints are the most accurate for a particular star system, which has hidden mass values of 0.009 solar masses, and a distance of 140 AU. Furthermore, the existence of these hidden mass companions may indicate a potential for discovering previously unknown brown dwarf binary systems.

Deep learning techniques have become essential tools for resolving intricate problems in computer science. Among these, the Variational Autoencoder (VAE) stands out as a widely used deep generative model that leverages the principles of Bayesian statistics. However, traditional VAEs have been found to rely heavily on the mean squared error loss function, which can lead to poor image reconstruction outcomes. This limitation is due to the mismatch between the likelihood of the observed data and the loss function, causing the network to focus on pixel values rather than overall image quality. This paper introduces a new optimization technique for VAEs, which combines a regularization approach with a novel loss function derived from the Sum of Squared Differences (SSD) metric, commonly employed in computer vision. By doing so, the proposed method aims to overcome the limitations of existing models, such as the loss of salient features and poor image quality, often observed in state-of-the-art VAEs. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through a series of experiments on various datasets.

The rapid growth of the Internet of Things has led to widespread deployment of IoT-enabled devices in our daily lives, including smart home gadgets and wearables. These IoT devices are vulnerable to cyber threats due to their interconnected nature and limited resources, making them targets for hackers who exploit their security flaws. To safeguard IoT devices, researchers have proposed blockchain technology, leveraging its distributed nature and transparent ledger system. However, blockchain solutions are not well-suited for IoT devices due to their high computational requirements. To address this, this paper proposes an enhanced private blockchain-based security protocol for securing smart home gadgets and wearables. This security protocol uses a consensus mechanism, a variant of the Proof-of-Stake algorithm, to optimize resource usage on IoT devices. Furthermore, the proposed solution employs a client-server architecture with a computational method to monitor smart home gadgets and wearables for enhanced functionality and user experience.

This research introduces an advanced method for quantizing likelihood ratios (L-values) using an artificial neural network (ANN) to achieve faster and more efficient coding. Traditional methods often employ fixed-bit quantization, but these can result in reduced coding performance due to the loss of information. In response, this paper proposes adaptive quantization using an ANN to determine the optimal number of bits for each L-value. This approach significantly reduces the total number of bits required, while also preserving more original data. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the method was tested with an ANN-based quantizer and a deep learning driven quantizer (DLQ) on various channels, including the binary symmetric channel and mixture Gaussian channel. By utilizing the ANN to calculate log-likelihood scores (LLS) for each quantization level, the proposed method outperforms traditional fixed-bit quantization techniques, particularly in terms of overall coding performance.

Upward planarity of flow graphs, where each edge's slope corresponds to its directional requirement, is studied in terms of its existence and drawing.  A new algorithm is developed to identify the parameters that limit the number of monotone and upward planar drawings of a given flow graph, along with a parameterized algorithm that finds a valid upward planar drawing if one exists.  The algorithm determines the maximum number of such drawings that can be created by partitioning the graph into specific components and analyzing their properties.  The research also explores the use of specific graph classes, such as trees and paths, as parameters for the problem and finds a parameterized algorithm that uses these classes as well as the number of sources and sinks in the graph.  The research proves the problem to be intractable when using the size of the sinks as a parameter and uses an incompressible structure to demonstrate this intractability.

Crowdsourced data is often marred by noise, which can be analyzed and quantified using uncertainty metrics. The complexity of crowdsourced data stems from its dual nature, where both the variability of human perception and the interplay of different methods contribute to discrepancies in answers. Traditional techniques to filter out human error are insufficient in accounting for the uncertainties inherent in different methods. In this research, we introduce a multi-faceted approach to tackle this issue, leveraging ensemble modeling, 'human softmax' distributions, and uncertainty quantification to establish a precise relationship between human perception and uncertainty. The proposed approach was tested on a 100,000+ item dataset and demonstrated its effectiveness in identifying and eliminating both human and model biases. The findings indicate that this approach can provide a reliable tool for analyzing and interpreting large-scale, noisy crowdsourced datasets.

We introduce novel upper bounds to the norm of transfer operators associated with dynamical systems, specifically those linked to the boundary of regions that experience exponential rate of dispersion of trajectories as semiflows evolve over time. These optimized transfer operators play a crucial role in establishing equivalence norms between various functional spaces, thus facilitating the investigation of physical measures' smoothness in relation to the Parry-Harrington method. The application of our approach is demonstrated through analysis of Beltrami flows in simply connected three-dimensional domains with an extremely steeply inclined boundary.

A covering array with minor strength-2 is a data structure used in software testing, denoted as a CA$_{\rm sm2}$, where any two columns in an $N \times t$ array have all possible values from $\mu^4$ subarrays. The minimum size of this array is represented as $\mathsf{sm2}(t, \mu)$. A unique matrix, called the quotient matrix, is used to analyze the properties of these arrays. The goal of this paper is to establish a relationship between the minimum size of these arrays and the maximum eigenvalue of the quotient matrix. Additionally, this paper introduces a new method for constructing these arrays.

Contest games, also known as Majorana games, involve multiple players with the same objectives, with outcomes dependent on their collective actions. In contest analysis, researchers typically assume flawless knowledge among players, with a common goal of achieving equilibrium. However, real-world scenarios rarely meet this standard, prompting an investigation into contests involving imperfect knowledge. A notable study, conducted by Bornholdt and Masuda, introduced a method for modeling contests as a quantum system, with a focus on how interconnected player states affect contest outcomes. Our research extends this work by analyzing contests with both low and high levels of interconnectedness, with a specific focus on the effects of measurement errors. We demonstrate that determining equilibria in these contests is a feasible computational task, with outcomes that can be either unique or non-unique, with a unique equilibrium leading to well-defined measurement errors and non-unique equilibria resulting in undefined measurement errors. Our study also highlights a notable phenomenon, with a specific threshold below which no stable points occur and above which stable points become ubiquitous, with a specific focus on how this behavior is influenced by contest structure and noise levels.

This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of a genetic algorithm in automatically replicating software crashes. To achieve this, we will compare the algorithm's results with the original study's findings under the same conditions, while employing a different implementation in Python. We will then assess the algorithm's capacity to identify the required inputs and match the original outputs. We will also consider the original code's potential influence on the results and the differences between our Python code and the Java original.

Theoretical models suggest a connection between the complex phase diagram of high-temperature cuprate superconductors and the intricate behavior of vortex lattices formed by quanta of magnetic flux. These models propose that vortex lattices undergo a series of transformations, shifting from a triangular pattern to a grid pattern as magnetic fields and temperatures change. This study utilizes scanning SQUID microscopy to directly visualize the triangular and square patterns of vortex arrangements in the $T_\textrm{c} = 95$ K cuprate, $\textrm{Bi}_2\textrm{Sr}_2\textrm{Ca}_2\textrm{Cu}_2\textrm{O}_{10+\delta}$, and demonstrates that the transition between these patterns is linked to the change from a single to a double square lattice of vortices. This transition is linked to the presence of paired vortices within the superconductor's grains and highlights the significant role of grain boundaries in shaping the material's complex phase diagram.

Researchers have discovered that the directional flow of thermal photons is sensitive to the angular momentum of the collision system and is influenced by the properties of the quark-gluon plasma. Through hydrodynamic simulations, they found that viscosity has a significant impact on this directional flow, especially when considering low angular momentum collisions. As a result, they can use measurements of this directional flow to make a precise prediction of the plasma's viscosity without relying on theoretical assumptions.

The kagome lattice is a common structure in both two and three-dimensional magnetic materials, often appearing in combination with a triangular lattice, as seen in materials like kagome and Tri-kagome metals. To address this, we developed a comprehensive model for kagome and triangular lattices that consider the effects of spin-rotation symmetry, inversion, and lattice translations. Our results show that only three distinct magnetic arrangements are possible in lattices with kagome and triangular patterns that satisfy all the relevant constraints, and we identified one arrangement with a three-fold rotation axis. Interestingly, we found that a three-fold magnetic arrangement is only feasible in kagome and tri-kagome lattices, but not in lattices with only triangular patterns. To validate our findings, we used numerical methods to study the behavior of the kagome and triangular lattices in the J_1-J_2 Heisenberg model. Our results show that the consistent model accurately predicts the magnetic behavior of these patterns.

In large-scale intervention studies, researchers often face a challenge of false positives when evaluating multiple interventions. To address this, the multi-arm intervention study framework is commonly used to control for false discoveries. However, the standard multivariate analysis assumes independence between interventions, which is not always the case. To address this limitation, a new method has been developed to calculate the FDR under dependence by using the r-dependent model. This approach allows for the identification of interventions with a low FDR even when dependencies exist. To further enhance the FDR control under the r-dependent model, the authors propose a new method called the rgFDR, which can be applied to datasets with regulated variables. This method is validated through theoretical proof and empirical evidence, and the results show that the rgFDR can improve FDR control compared to other methods.

The anomaly in the value of a muon's magnetic moment and the mass difference in muons can be resolved by the type-X two Higgs doublet model. This model, in which both charged Higgs and Higgs boson interact with up-type and down-type quarks as well as charged leptons, is analyzed in detail. Specifically, the model's parameters are constrained by Higgs mass and coupling data from the LHC and precision electroweak measurements, and then its one-loop corrections to the muon's magnetic moment and mass difference in muons are calculated. Results show that for light Higgs boson masses, the model's predictions for the mass difference in muons can be dominated by the CP-even Higgs boson, whereas its predictions for a muon's magnetic moment are dominated by the CP-odd Higgs boson, ultimately resolving the anomalies in a manner consistent with the experimental data from the LHC.

Data analysis is greatly facilitated by metadata, which enables efficient data retrieval and is highly sought after in various fields such as agriculture, geology, and space exploration. Generating machine-readable metadata is a labor-intensive process, but search engine technology can help bridge this gap by matching search queries to database metadata. Implementing automatic metadata generation through search query suggestion, however, poses significant challenges due to the limitations of traditional search engines. Our research introduces SWIFTER, a novel system that leverages crowd-sourced input to generate multiple relevant synonyms for each concept, ultimately enhancing the ability to discover new metadata. Our results demonstrate that SWIFTER is capable of generating high-quality alternatives, comparable to human-generated metadata.

Effective communication relies heavily on synchronizing speech production and reception. Research has identified that people with autism spectrum disorder often struggle with conversational synchronization, which may contribute to their social challenges. To better understand and potentially rectify these challenges, researchers are developing tools to measure synchronization distances between speakers. These tools, currently limited to analyzing synchronized audio or text, have now been extended to include more advanced deep neural models that can process speech as a unified representation. These new models, which come with potential biases, have been tested using synthetic data that simulates synchronized speech. By analyzing this data, researchers have discovered that some distance measures perform better than others and that training methods can help mitigate potential biases. Ultimately, these models have shown that they can successfully learn a speaker's identity and estimate synchronization distances, paving the way for future research in understanding communication disorders like autism.

Researchers working in the field of sub-millimeter astronomy are increasingly utilizing various data formats, including images and spectral data. To facilitate the efficient sharing of these data among researchers, specialized online tools are required. An open-source suite of tools has been developed to enable researchers to interactively visualize data in a web browser without installing any additional software. This toolset, known as RCSEDv2, is designed to be both user-friendly and customizable, allowing for the incorporation of new features and functionality. As such, it provides a versatile and adaptable platform for sub-millimeter astronomers to collaborate and share their findings.

Recent research has demonstrated that self-supervised learning methods can be effective for Temporal Action Segmentation (TAS) tasks that have not been extensively annotated. A novel approach, introduced in this paper, utilizes self-supervised learning to discover spatially and temporally coherent action patterns from video data. These patterns are generated by breaking down the temporal action information embedded in video data. A distinct characteristic of this method is its ability to derive spatial patterns from videos, unlike other self-supervised TAS approaches. To evaluate its performance, we created a new benchmark dataset, SSCAP-DA15K, which consists of video clips randomly selected from the DAVIS-15K dataset. Our experimental results show that the learned patterns can be used for TAS, achieving a mIoU of 36.9% on DAVIS-15K, surpassing existing methods by 0.9%. Additionally, we established a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the effectiveness of various self-supervised learning methods on TAS.

Using the present algebra, we've identified three pentaquark states, including two with hidden charm, and found their relevant operators. An operator connecting the algebra to these states functions as a selection tool, allowing the formation of specific pentaquark states and in turn, the decays of the $\bar{b}$ quark, ultimately yielding states like charmonium, and mesons like $D$ and $J/\psi$ particles. This has enabled the determination of production rates for pentaquark states in both $\bar{b}$-annihilation reactions and $B$-meson decays. Furthermore, we've analyzed the mass spectrum of the pentaquark states, including their masses and quantum numbers, as well as the potential for identifying these states in a signal over the background of a charmonium and a $D$-meson in $\bar{b}$-annihilation reactions. Additionally, we've found that a specific type of nonfactorizable amplitude is the primary factor influencing the $D$-wave pentaquark state in the decays of the $B$-meson.

In computer science education, feedback is a crucial element for both students and educators. 
While traditional review methods are effective, they can be time-consuming and may not be suitable for large classes. 
A more efficient approach, inquiry-based conceptual feedback (IBCF), has been developed to provide formative feedback in a concise multiple-choice format. 
This study compares IBCF with two traditional evaluation methods, code review, and traditional conceptual evaluation. 
The experiment involved a total of 100 participants, including 20 students receiving IBCF feedback and 80 students divided into two groups of 40, where one group received code review and the other traditional conceptual evaluation. 
A comprehensive online survey was conducted to analyze the effectiveness of the three evaluation methods. 
The results indicate that IBCF is effective in promoting learning, and can be a valuable tool for educators in providing formative feedback to a large number of students in a concise and efficient manner.

Domain adaptation is a machine learning technique that allows us to apply a model trained on a source domain with labeled data to a target domain with limited or no labeled data.  Recently, the idea of theory transfer has gained attention, where theoretical models are transferred to the target domain.  However, theory transfer is more complex than traditional supervised domain adaptation because theoretical models are often abstract and may not have direct applications in the target domain.  Additionally, the target domain in theory transfer tasks often has limited data, making it difficult to apply traditional domain adaptation methods.  To address these challenges, we propose a semi-supervised theory transfer approach that can effectively transfer knowledge from a source domain with limited data to a target domain with limited or no labeled data.  Our method involves two steps: 1) Coarse-to-fine matching, where we match the elements of the source and target theories based on their abstract meanings and then refine the matches using the abstract concepts in the theories; 2) Leveraging the matched theories to improve the target domain's performance through knowledge distillation and semi-supervised learning.  Our approach can adapt to different scenarios, including fully-supervised, semi-supervised, and unsupervised target domains, and can handle varying amounts of labeled data.  Our method outperforms state-of-the-art domain adaptation methods and achieves significant improvements in challenging scenarios with limited data, such as transferring from a simplified physics model to a more complex real-world physics model with limited data.

A novel space propulsion system, utilizing gas core air-breathing jet engines, is proposed as a means of transportation to the Outer Limiting Orbital Region (OLO) and beyond. This system is particularly well-suited for remote exploration missions to diverse celestial bodies, such as asteroids, moons, and planets, rather than for rapid transportation. By harnessing the energy of a nuclear reactor, this propulsion system can draw oxygen from the atmosphere of visited worlds to minimize the need to carry onboard oxidizers, thus reducing costs. Additionally, this technology can be employed to investigate the atmospheres of unknown celestial bodies, providing a broader range of applications.

One of the significant challenges in neutrino astronomy, particularly for the next generation of neutrino detectors, involves detecting and localizing neutrino-charged particle interactions within large target volumes. Current methods for this task rely on traditional machine learning techniques, but we propose an alternative using neural networks that incorporate physical knowledge about the underlying neutrino interaction processes. Specifically, we develop an analytical model that maps the target volume coordinates to a multi-dimensional weighted graph, which we then use to train neural networks for predicting charged particle directions. Our domain-informed graph neural network, designed for 3D directional classification, achieves state-of-the-art results on public datasets, demonstrating improved performance over existing methods when evaluating the localization of neutrino-induced interactions within large detectors.

The study of substellar exoplanet atmospheres involves analyzing their unique spectral characteristics, which are influenced by various chemical components. As our understanding of these spectral features expands, the need for readily accessible, accurate spectral models and databases becomes increasingly important. In response to this, the EXOPLINES project aims to provide a comprehensive collection of molecular absorption coefficients for six key molecules, specifically H2O, CH4, NH3, and CO, tailored to the atmospheres of brown dwarfs and gas giant exoplanets. In this paper, the objectives of the EXOPLINES project are outlined, the results of the initial testing of these databases are presented, and the initial contributions of the project are introduced, including the spectral models, cross-sections, and the associated computational tools.

This text outlines our key insights on the role of grounding in answer set programming.  We initially discuss why grounding is essential for the satisfiability check and then explore how it facilitates reduct computation.  Our analysis on how current solvers handle grounding informs our perspective on existing and potential future approaches.  Furthermore, we examine how grounding interacts with other computational stages and identify opportunities for reducing the impact of grounding, either by integrating it with other phases or by applying reusability strategies across the different possible orderings of satisfiability and computation by model.

In this paper, we introduce a resource theory of quantum operations, which is based on a convex subset of all quantum operations. Our resource theory is defined without any restrictions and thus encompasses all the resource quantifiers that we have developed for specialized models, such as entanglement theories with restricted operations. Our resource monotone is defined as the minimum number of copies of the input operation required to approximate a specified target operation within a specified distance. Our main result demonstrates that, with a large number of operations, this resource monotone can be quantified by a single formula that applies to any quantum resource theory. This result is proven by constructing a way to produce a standardized, canonical form of the input and target operations by consuming a minimal amount of resources. We apply this result to analyze the resource theory of channel discrimination, revealing a simple formula for a recently proposed resource quantifier, which we show is equivalent to a maximum mutual information between the channel's encoded and decoded states.

We develop a fundamental framework to evaluate a model's predictions or a specific distribution that captures the essence of a dataset. The framework considers various moments, each representing an essential aspect of uncertainty. The framework allows us to convert the accuracy of predictions based on these moments into a specific scoring metric. The most effective scoring metric for this purpose is identified through an optimization process. The superior scoring metric exhibits a specific set of properties that make it ideal for model comparison. The mechanism behind this optimization process is explained using a specific utility function. The optimization process is further simplified in the case of a particular set of moments, leading to a specific utility function. The effectiveness of this optimization process is demonstrated using a variety of examples, including a comparison between different machine learning models.

In a non-stationary time series context, multi-dimensional data is analyzed where the underlying distribution has a non-stable underlying structure. A novel method is developed to estimate the dependence parameters of such time series, even when individual data points are unknown. It's demonstrated that the non-stable and non-stationary nature of the time series can be effectively handled under specific conditions. A large-sample normality proof for the estimator is established, and a consistent rate of convergence for one particular estimator is identified. This method's performance is validated through multi-asset log-returns data from a financial context.

Currently, there's ongoing debate about the best error correction codes to use in the context of fault-tolerant quantum computing, with no consensus reached yet. A prominent class of codes, known as quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, offer a promising solution. These codes can achieve arbitrary logical error rates while scaling across any plane, provided they have an appropriate level of connectivity for their check constraints. However, high connectivity often leads to complex decoding processes with time complexity that increases quadratically with system size. To address this complexity issue, our study presents an infinite family of quantum LDPC code constructions that support a linear number of qubits per check, while still maintaining high connectivity and allowing for efficient linear time decoding. Additionally, we've also proposed another set of constructions with lower connectivity requirements. These innovative codes have the potential to significantly advance quantum error correction capabilities, paving the way for more efficient fault-tolerant quantum computing.

A vertex subset S of a graph G is considered a distance-r controlling set if every vertex not in S is within a distance of at most r from a vertex in S. The minimum size of such a set is denoted by $\gamma_r(G)$. Specifically, when r equals 1, this concept becomes the traditional dominating set. Researchers have shown that for certain maximum degree $\Delta$ graphs, the upper bound of $\gamma_r(G)$ can be determined. By considering the sparsity of a sparse high-girth graph, this research provides a specific bound for $\gamma_r(G)$ where the maximum distance to the nearest set member is reduced to $O(\log_{\Delta-1} n)$, and this reduction is an improvement over previous results.

We have developed a theoretical framework for understanding how the effective mass of a quasiparticle is connected to localized states at the system's boundaries. This is achieved by applying the inverse participation ratio to models with and without time-reversal symmetry. Our analysis reveals that when time-reversal symmetry is absent, a perturbation based on the effective mass leads to the exponential decay of the quasiparticle mass at the boundary. The accuracy of this approximation is verified by comparing it with numerical solutions. Furthermore, our research shows that under time-reversal symmetry, the relationship between the bulk quasiparticle mass and boundary states becomes more complex. We have also investigated how the topological phase transitions in a four-dimensional lattice model are affected by disorder, and found that the change in effective mass is directly linked to the appearance of delocalized boundary states.

Recent searches for highly ionizing tracks at the CMS have yielded interesting findings that align with localized decay points within metastable long-lived particles, particularly neutralinos from supersymmetry. Analysis of 138 fb^-1 of data from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV has been conducted, resulting in the exclusion of several local supersymmetry mass regions. Notably, scenarios where the supersymmetry mass spectrum is heavy, exceeding 1 TeV, have been ruled out based on local analysis and may also be excluded globally.

Our proposed technique, Bright Field Neural Visualization, involves a transparent, brightly lit volume that is rendered in real-time and is filled with micro-textures. This approach is similar to light fields but differs in its rendering process. Our method offers increased scene visibility and is particularly effective in highlighting high-contrast features. Our pipeline includes a novel, efficient rendering technique that leverages the parallel processing capabilities of GPUs to quickly produce high-quality results. We have thoroughly tested and compared our approach with other techniques, demonstrating its effectiveness and superior visual quality through various evaluations and examples.

This paper presents the second-year results from the SOAR telescope's CFIS, where the instrument conducted 1,500 hours of observations. Interferometric measurements between the SOAR and Calar Alto 3.5m telescopes yielded a total of 1,020 new spectral binary star measurements. These data have been added to the CFBIS catalog, showcasing the binary systems identified in this year's observations. Furthermore, the paper outlines the instrument's performance and outlines the planned activities for Year 3.

Chiral algebras, as introduced by Brinzei and Witten, are a mathematical framework that has significant connections to various aspects of supersymmetric theories. In the context of four-dimensional super-Yang-Mills theory, they are linked to specific holomorphic components of MHV amplituhedron data and super-Penner-Horowitz-Witten forms. A new class of chiral algebras, referred to as heavenly chiral algebras, is now defined based on two-dimensional integrable structures, and their properties are shown to be related to SK-equivalence in amplituhedra. This relationship leads to a chiral form of the amplitude/Witten Hamiltonian duality and, in turn, is connected to the integrable structure found in the Yangian. Chiral wave functions derived from these algebras are demonstrated to be related to the Witten Hamiltonian, and their poles correspond to holomorphic components of on-shell amplitudes. These poles are also found to be in correspondence with the integrable components of the Yangian.

In the framework of the general two Higgs doublet model, we've carried out probability analyses for flavour irregularities and the anomalous magnetic moment discrepancies of the muon, focusing on scenarios where Higgs boson mass splittings are small ($\lesssim 100$ GeV). Our research, particularly in Type I and Type II models, indicates a low likelihood of one scenario being associated with another, particularly when up and down quark flavour irregularities are considered, but we found that up and down quark scenarios often overlap. However, we found a strong correlation between muon anomalous magnetic moment discrepancies and flavour irregularities within the same quark sector. This strong correlation led us to identify preferred parameter spaces, particularly in specific two Higgs doublet models.

This study explores a stochastic system of particles in a fluid, where particle movement is influenced by the fluid's complex dynamics represented as a time-varying function. We examine this system in the context of a probabilistic representation of a stochastic differential equation, incorporating the fluid's dynamics. We also investigate an analogous system in the context of a functional probabilistic differential equation, derived from a measure-valued process tracking the particles' spatial distribution.

Boson sampling is a prominent quantum computing application that can be efficiently executed on quantum systems but is challenging for classical computers to simulate. By utilizing single photons as quantum bits, the sampling process enables control over quantum interference between photons while ion sources remain in classical states. We investigate how boson sampling impacts the entanglement of the process and derive an analytical expression for calculating entanglement entropy. Our analysis demonstrates that while interference creates entanglement, it does not guarantee a full quantum state. We provide a quantitative measure of entanglement generated by boson sampling and derive its upper limit. Furthermore, we show that this entanglement can be estimated by measuring only one mode after boson sampling.

To successfully master intricate tasks, humans and animals rely on recalling detailed sequences of events. These sequences, however, are often complex and difficult to analyze due to their length. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel method for efficiently encoding and recalling extensive sequences. This approach involves using neural networks to condense raw data into a more manageable format, which can then be further simplified by human experts. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this strategy through an application in life science, where we analyze brain activity patterns in rats. These activation sequences, when studied, reveal that even highly condensed sequences retain the capacity to accurately predict original behaviors, while also highlighting the value of human expertise in understanding these complex sequences.

Recurrent neural networks, particularly when used in partially observable environments, have a particular strength in capturing and retaining information about past events. We delve into the nature of this memory retention, examining how the structure of these networks enables the storage of relevant details despite limited external inputs. Our research reveals that certain types of recurrent networks can effectively function as belief systems, accurately representing their uncertain knowledge. We also explore the relationship between the structural characteristics of these networks and their capacity to form beliefs, using both a mathematical approach and simulations. We further investigate the practical implications of this discovery, demonstrating how it can be used to develop more resilient and predictable recurrent networks, even in complex and uncertain real-world scenarios.

Human action recognition is becoming an increasingly important area of research with applications in security, self-driving cars, and robotics. However, most existing methods struggle to detect the exact start and stop times of actions. In contrast, detecting the location of actions within a video is more challenging than action recognition itself. Recent advances in reading-comprehension models have led to the development of weakly-guided action detection tasks, which use specific guidance to locate actions within video sequences. Despite this progress, identifying suitable guidance frames remains difficult, particularly when only a coarse localization is available. To address this issue, our paper introduces a novel approach that leverages graph convolutional networks to identify context-rich frames that aid in action detection. Our method involves using multiple GCN models to process different types of graph representations, which capture various features such as semantic information and visual characteristics. By analyzing the changes in these graph representations, our model identifies the most informative frames that serve as guidance for detecting actions. Our results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets.

The 2021 Image Similarity Challenge brought together a global community of researchers to address the issue of image similarity and object recognition. Held as part of the second MLS Competition, over 130 teams from 35 countries and regions participated, showcasing the international significance of the challenge. This paper details the specific tasks, evaluation methods, and results of the challenge, as well as presents fresh insights and perspectives on state-of-the-art image similarity models.
